summary: The direct object — what is eaten, drunk, bought, liked or cooked — comes after the verb. Hebrew nouns have no case endings, but a **definite** direct object gets the small word אֶת (et) in front of it: הוּא אוֹכֵל תַּפּוּחַ “he eats an apple” — הוּא אוֹכֵל אֶת הַתַּפּוּחַ “he eats the apple”. Definite means: a noun with הַ, a two-word noun whose second word has הַ (אֶת אֲרוּחַת הַבֹּקֶר), a noun with הַ + שֶׁלִּי … or הַזֶּה (אֶת הַקָּפֶה שֶׁלּוֹ), a name, or a pronoun. An indefinite object has no marker at all. אֶת is not translated; it is Hebrew’s counterpart of an accusative — and it works exactly like the Turkish accusative -(y)ı, which you know: elma yiyor / elmayı yiyor. With a pronoun אֶת takes endings: אוֹתִי “me”, אוֹתוֹ “him, it”, אוֹתָהּ “her, it” … In standard Hebrew the thing after יֵשׁ / אֵין is a subject, so it has no אֶת. Objects with prepositions (to, for, with) and the indirect object come later (S11–S13, C03).

blocks.title: אֶת = “the following object is definite”
blocks.text: Hebrew marks the direct object only when it is definite — the same rule as the Turkish accusative: elma yiyorum “I eat an apple” / elmayı yiyorum “I eat the apple”.

blocks.title: No אֶת before an indefinite object
blocks.text: *הוּא אוֹכֵל אֶת תַּפּוּחַ is wrong: without הַ there is no אֶת — הוּא אוֹכֵל תַּפּוּחַ.

blocks.title: אֶת or אַתְּ?
blocks.text: Without vowel marks both are written את: אֶת (et) marks the object, אַתְּ (at) is “you” to a woman. The sentence tells you which: אַתְּ אוֹכֶלֶת אֶת הַלֶּחֶם “you (f.) eat the bread”.

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: What is eaten, drunk, bought, liked?
Does it have הַ, a name, a pronoun?

askYourself: Does the verb have a direct object (what is eaten, drunk, bought, liked, cooked)?
Is the object definite — with הַ, a definite second word, a name, a pronoun? → אֶת before it.
Is it indefinite (no article)? → nothing before it.
Is it a pronoun? → אֶת with an ending: אוֹתוֹ, אוֹתָהּ …
Is it after יֵשׁ / אֵין? → standard Hebrew puts no אֶת there.
Is there a preposition (to, with, for)? → that is not a direct object (S11).
steps: Definite object: אֶת + the definite noun.

traps: *הוּא אוֹכֵל אֶת תַּפּוּחַ — אֶת only before a definite object.
*אֲנִי אוֹהֵב הַסָּלָט — a definite object needs אֶת: אֲנִי אוֹהֵב אֶת הַסָּלָט.
In a two-word noun הַ goes on the second word, but אֶת stands before the whole: אֶת אֲרוּחַת הָעֶרֶב.
*אֲנִי אוֹהֵב אֶת הוּא — the object pronoun is one word: אוֹתוֹ.
אֶת “(object)” and אַתְּ “you (f.)” look the same without vowels: את.
The subject never takes אֶת: הַיֶּלֶד אוֹכֵל אֶת הַתַּפּוּחַ.

seeAlso.note: Arabic marks every direct object with the accusative ending -a / -an (أَكَلَ التُّفَّاحَةَ, أَكَلَ تُفَّاحَةً), definite or not; Hebrew marks only the definite one, and with a separate word, אֶת.
German puts every direct object in the accusative, seen mostly on the article (einen Apfel / den Apfel); Hebrew adds אֶת only before a definite object.
Chinese has no object marker here: word order alone (我吃苹果) shows the object.
